questions.question: Describe the parts of a climate graph and explain how to read a temperature and a rainfall value accurately.
questions.expected_answer: The horizontal axis shows the twelve months, J to D. One vertical axis shows temperature in °C and the other rainfall in mm; some graphs swap the sides, so read the labels first. Temperature is a line, with points plotted in the middle of each month, because it changes continuously; sometimes there are maximum and minimum lines. Rainfall is bars, one per month, because it is a monthly total. The title names the place, often with latitude, longitude and altitude, and a box may give the annual total and mean. To read a value, find the month, go up to the line or the top of the bar, then read across to the correct axis, using a ruler. The figures are 30-year averages, not a single year's weather.

questions.question: Using Station A's figures, describe its climate with calculations and identify its type.
questions.expected_answer: Temperatures range from 13 °C in July and August to 22 °C in February, an annual range of 22 − 13 = 9 °C, with a mean of about 17 °C; winters are mild, above 10 °C, and summers warm, below 25 °C. Total rainfall is 15 + 17 + 20 + 41 + 69 + 93 + 82 + 77 + 40 + 30 + 14 + 17 = 515 mm. The wettest month is June with 93 mm and the driest November with 14 mm. May to August receive 321 mm, about 62 percent of the total, since 321 ÷ 515 ≈ 0.62. The tallest bars lie under the lowest part of the line, so rain falls in winter. It is a Mediterranean climate, like Cape Town's: warm, dry summers under subtropical high pressure and mild, wet winters from cold fronts in the westerlies.

questions.question: Compare Station A and Station B, using figures, and explain the difference in their rainfall seasons.
questions.expected_answer: Both have a mean annual temperature of about 17 °C. Station A's range is 9 °C, whereas Station B's is 11 °C, suggesting B is further inland. Station A receives 515 mm, about 62 percent from May to August, with its wettest month June at 93 mm; Station B receives 671 mm, about 85 percent from October to March, with its wettest month January at 135 mm and only 3 mm in July. A has winter rain because cold fronts in the westerlies reach the south-western Cape when the pressure belts shift north, while summer brings dry high pressure. B has summer rain because summer heating causes convection and moist Indian Ocean air brings thunderstorms, while in winter high pressure over the interior brings sinking, dry air.
